PAPER: Safe Multi-Robotic Arm Interaction via 3D Convex Shapes Ali Umut Kaypaka,∗, Shiqing Weia, Prashanth Krishnamurthya, Farshad Khorramia aElectrical and Computer Engineering Department, Tandon School of Engineering, New York University, Brooklyn, 11201, NY, USA Abstract Inter-robot collisions pose a significant safety risk when multiple robotic arms operate in close proximity. We present an online collision avoidance methodology leveraging High-Order Control Barrier Functions (HOCBFs) constructed for safe interactions among 3D convex shapes to address this issue. While prior works focused on using Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) for human–robotic arm and single-arm collision avoidance, we explore the problem of collision avoidance between multiple robotic arms operating in a shared space. In our methodology, we utilize the proposed HOCBFs as centralized and decentralized safety filters. These safety filters are compat- ible with many nominal controllers and ensure safety without significantly restricting the robots’ workspace. A key challenge in implementing these filters is the computational overhead caused by the large number of safety constraints and the computation of a Hessian matrix per constraint. We address this challenge by employing numerical differentiation methods to ap- proximate computationally intensive terms. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through extensive simulation studies and real-world experi- ments with Franka Research 3 robotic arms. The project video is available at this link. Introduction The deployment of robots in unstructured dynamic environments neces- sitates effective collision prevention mechanisms. Various approaches have been proposed for this purpose, including Model Predictive Control (MPC)- based safety strategies [1, 2] and CBF-based methods [3–8]. CBF-based methods have received attention because of their ability to enforce forward invariance of safety sets while maintaining computational efficiency in many scenarios. Leveraging these properties, recent research has extensively ex- plored their application in inter-robot collision avoidance, particularly for safe navigation in mobile robot systems [4–7]. However, despite the impor- tance of multi-robotic arm interaction in specific applications [9, 10], CBF- based safety certificates for ensuring safe multi-robotic arm interaction re- main largely unexplored. This work addresses this gap by investigating the application of CBFs that enhance safety during multi-robotic arm interac- tions and collaborative tasks. CBFs are often used as constraints in Quadratic Programming (QP) to enforce safety [11]. The QP aims to keep the control input as close to the nominal controller as possible while obeying the safety constraints. To gen- eralize this framework for systems whose relative degree with respect to the constraint function is higher than one, HOCBFs were introduced [12, 13]. Our methodology is built on this concept by employing HOCBFs for colli- sion avoidance among 3D convex shapes, as introduced in [3]. We extend the use of HOCBFs from single robotic arm collision avoidance to inter-robotic arm collision avoidance by utilizing them in pairwise robotic arm dynamics. The key challenge in utilizing HOCBFs constructed for safe interactions among 3D convex shapes in multi-robotic arms, compared to a single arm, is the increased computational overhead. This arises from calculating more constraints at every sampling time. Additionally, in multi-robot settings, all the 3D convex shapes used in the HOCBFs are dynamic. This further in- tensifies the computational burden. We address this issue by approximating computationally intensive terms via numerical derivative filters. Our contri- butions in this paper are summarized as follows: • Developing HOCBFs that ensure robot safety in multi-robotic arm set- tings and utilizing them in centralized and decentralized paradigms; • Addressing the computational challenges of deploying these HOCBFs 2 byestimatingthecomputationallyintensivetermswithnumericalderiva- tive filters; • Validating the proposed method through extensive simulations and real-world experiments. 2. Related works CBFs in inter-robot collision avoidance: The use of CBFs to pre- vent collisions in multi-robot systems is an active research area, with various methodologies proposed for different scenarios [4–8]. For instance, central- ized and decentralized CBF-based safety filters for planar mobile robots were introduced in [4]. A CBF-based methodology was developed for the safe con- trol of drone swarms in [6, 14]. In addition, a distributed controller for the safenavigationofmobilerobotswasproposedin[8]. Similarly, HOCBFswere employed to generate safety-assured trajectories for multiple legged robots in [5]. However, extending these approaches to the multi-robotic arm setting is not straightforward. Although some work [15, 16] applied CBFs to ensure safe human-multiple robot arm interaction, they did not address possible collisions between robot bodies. This is the first work applying CBFs for collision avoidance among multiple robotic arms. Inter-robotic arm collision avoidance: Collision handling between robotic arms can be categorized into online [17–19] and offline [20, 21] meth- ods. Offline methods predefine commands and trajectories, while online methods address collisions in real time. Various online strategies have been explored. For example, collision maps were utilized to detect potential col- lisions and schedule command execution times while preserving the path in [18]. Nonlinear MPC was employed for online trajectory planning, incorpo- rating collision avoidance into the optimization constraints in [19]. Addition- ally, a motion planning method based on Soft Actor-Critic was proposed in [17] to prevent collisions in dual-robotic arms. In contrast to these approaches, we introduce a CBF-based method de- signed as a seamless filtering layer compatible with any nominal controller. Unlike these methods, our approach provides reactive collision avoidance. It modifies the nominal controller’s inputs (and thus the offline-generated tra- jectories) only when necessary to prevent potential collisions, thereby pre- serving the intended high-level task execution. Moreover, our method com- plements offline collision avoidance approaches, preventing robot collisions 3 that may arise due to unexpected changes in the task environment after the initial trajectory has been planned. 3. In the centralized filter, QP infeasibility, i.e. an empty feasible set, can theoretically arise, although we did not encounter this situation in any experiment. A typical place where it may become infeasible is in highly cluttered environments where a robot’s movement is prevented by multiple surrounding robots. Even when the cen- tralized QP remains feasible, one or more QPs in the decentralized filters may become infeasible under the same scenario. This occurs because the decentral- ized formulation shrinks the feasible sets to decouple the shared problem into independent subproblems. When QP infeasibility is observed, a fail-safe mode that halts all robots by applying accelerations opposite to their joint velocities is activated. Since the safety filters already bound joint speeds, this braking action stops the robots before contact. However, activating the fail-safe mode interrupts the high-level task being executed by the nominal controller and requires new high-level planning before resuming operation. In practice, we observed no QP infeasibility with the centralized filter and only a few cases with the decentralized filters; see Sec. 7 for details. 6. Furthermore, the need to define θ as a 14- dimensional vector for two moving objects—compared to 7 dimensions for a moving robot and a static obstacle—further amplifies the computational burden of HOCBF computations. This θ i k j l Hessian is required to compute the term θ ˙T (∇2α⋆(θ ))θ ˙ . We re- fer to this term as Hessian contribution thr i oku j lgho θ ut the i k j r l ema i i k n j l der of the paper. To alleviate the computational burden, we propose approximating (∇2α⋆(θ ))θ ˙ = d (∇ α⋆(θ )) via numerical differentiation. This nu- θ i k j l i k j l dt θ i k j l merical derivative is obtained by using the gradient computed at the current time step together with gradients from previous time steps. The approxi- mated Hessian contribution is then obtained by taking the dot product of this numerical derivative with θ ˙ . Note that the gradient ∇ α⋆(θ ) is i j θ i j k l k l already computed as part of other terms in the HOCBF formulation, so no additional gradient evaluation is necessary. Since real robot sensor read- 16 ings can be noisy and susceptible to environmental perturbations, we use a robust numerical differentiation filter, the Savitzky-Golay filter [26], in our methodology, where its parameters can be tuned according to the noise level. The Savitzky–Golay filter is characterized by two hyperparameters: the window length and the polynomial order. It fits a polynomial of the chosen ordertothemostrecentwindowofdatausingleastsquaresandcomputesthe derivative from the fitted curve. These hyperparameters affect the accuracy of the estimated Hessian contribution. An excessively large window length produces overly smoothed and lagged derivatives that fail to capture rapid changes. Conversely, a small window makes the filter sensitive to the noise in the signal. Higher-order polynomials capture complex trends but are more noise-sensitive, while lower orders offer better robustness against noise. In our implementation, we use a second-degree polynomial and select the win- dow length based on the expected noise level. Our proposed safety method operates robustly for a reasonable range of these hyperparameter values, in- dicating low sensitivity to their precise selection. Nonetheless, inappropriate hyperparameter choices can amplify derivative estimation errors, distort the estimated Hessian contribution, and ultimately compromise safety. Additional evidence for the method’s accuracy is pre- sented in Sec. 7, where the numerical estimation of the Hessian contribution does not compromise the safety of the robots. Conclusion We presented HOCBF-based safety constraints to prevent inter-robotic arm collisions. Using these constraints, we developed centralized, decen- tralized, and relaxed-decentralized filters. We addressed the computational overhead of HOCBFs by introducing an efficient estimation method based on numerical derivation. We validated the effectiveness of the proposed safety approach through simulation and real-robot experiments. In these experi- ments, we observed that decentralized filtering can suffer from QP infeasibil- ity in certain scenarios. Although relaxation mitigated this issue, it did not fully resolve it. Future work will focus on addressing this issue and applying the method in more challenging environments, including mobile robots with robotic arms. JSON: Name: hocbf_multi_arm_3d Title: High-order control barrier function safety filters for multi-robotic-arm collision avoidance using 3D convex-shape representations Short Hypothesis: Applying high-order control barrier function (HOCBF) safety filters constructed from 3D convex-shape scaling functions with numerically estimated Hessian contributions to multi-robotic-arm controllers will (causally) reduce inter-robot collision incidence to zero under tested trajectories while increasing mean task-tracking error by no more than 10% and maintaining a median control update rate ≥ 200 Hz compared with the same nominal controllers without HOCBF filtering. Related Work: Existing approaches to inter-robot collision avoidance include offline motion planners, model predictive control (MPC)-based online planners, and control-barrier-function (CBF) based safety filters. Offline planners guarantee feasibility for precomputed trajectories but cannot handle unforeseen perturbations. MPC enforces constraints online but is computationally heavy and less suitable for high-dimensional articulated arms at high update rates. CBF methods enforce forward-invariant safety sets with low computational cost for many low-dimensional systems and have been extended to high-order CBFs (HOCBFs) for relative-degree constraints; prior CBF/HOCBF work has focused on mobile robots, aerial swarms, legged robots, human–robot interaction, or single-arm obstacle avoidance. Limitations in prior methods include: poor scalability when the number of pairwise constraints grows with multiple articulated arms; lack of practical handling for HOCBF terms that require expensive second-derivative (Hessian) evaluations for 3D convex-shape interactions; limited decentralized feasibility guarantees and instances of QP infeasibility; and sparse real-robot validations at high control rates. Abstract: Inter-robot collisions are a critical safety concern when multiple robotic arms operate in overlapping workspaces. We propose a real-time safety-filtering pipeline that uses high-order control barrier functions (HOCBFs) defined on 3D convex-shape scaling functions (ellipsoids) to guarantee forward-invariance of pairwise separation constraints between robot links and end-effectors. To make HOCBF deployment tractable for multiple arms, we introduce a numerical differentiation strategy to estimate the Hessian-dependent term that otherwise dominates computation, enabling centralized and decentralized quadratic-programming (QP) safety filters compatible with arbitrary nominal controllers. The main contributions are: (1) construction of HOCBFs for pairwise 3D convex-shape interactions among articulated arms; (2) a computationally efficient numerical estimation method for Hessian contributions that preserves safety properties in practice; and (3) a comprehensive experimental evaluation including simulation and real Franka Research 3 arms demonstrating collision avoidance, controller compatibility, and runtime scalability. We expect this pipeline to reduce collision incidence under reactive control while retaining nominal task execution and achieving higher control update rates than analytic-Hessian implementations. Experiments: Datasets and environments: (1) Simulation: MuJoCo environments replicating Franka Research 3 kinematics and dynamics with 2, 4, and 8 robots in overlapping workspaces. Each robot modeled with 7 joints and four ellipsoidal primitives (last three links + end-effector). (2) Real-world: two Franka Research 3 arms mounted with overlapping workspaces. Trajectories/tasks: (A) intersecting circular and linear end-effector trajectories designed to cause collisions absent safety; (B) coordinated pick-and-place with intersecting handover points; (C) randomized waypoint-following sequences. Baselines: (i) nominal inverse-dynamics controller without safety filter; (ii) MPC-based online collision-avoidance controller tuned to real-time limits; (iii) first-order CBF-based safety filter applied per-link (where applicable); (iv) HOCBF with analytically computed Hessian (when feasible). Methods to evaluate: centralized-HOCBF-QP, decentralized-HOCBF-QP, decentralized-HOCBF-relaxed-QP; each with analytic Hessian (when available) and with numerical Hessian-estimation (Savitzky–Golay) variants. Solver and hardware: OSQP solver; measure on two hardware configurations: high performance CPU (24-core i9) and medium CPU (8–16 cores). Metrics: collision rate (binary per trial), minimum inter-body distance distribution, QP infeasibility rate, mean and 95th-percentile task-tracking error (Euclidean end-effector error), mean control-deviation norm (||u_safe - u_nom||), average per-HOCBF computation time, overall control loop update rate (median and variance), actuator effort (integral of squared torques), and safety filter intervention frequency. Statistical protocol: for each setup, run 100 independent trials per method/task/noise condition. Report means, standard errors, and perform pairwise statistical tests (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank) against the nominal baseline. Ablation studies: (A) analytic Hessian vs. numerical Hessian estimation (vary Savitzky–Golay window length and polynomial order); (B) centralized vs decentralized vs relaxed decentralized filters (vary responsibility coefficient c); (C) scalability sweep: measure runtime, update rate, and collision rate as number of robots increases (2,4,8); (D) noise sensitivity: inject Gaussian sensor noise at low/medium/high levels and measure effect on HOCBF values and collision rate. Success criteria: statistically significant reduction in collisions to zero (or to the detection limit) compared to nominal baseline, while keeping mean tracking error increase ≤ 10% and median control update rate ≥ 200 Hz in the target hardware condition. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: (1) QP infeasibility in decentralized filters under dense clutter or tight mutual constraints; (2) numerical derivative estimation errors (filter lag or amplification of noise) causing inaccurate Hessian contributions and potential violation of HOCBF inequalities; (3) solver numerical instability with large numbers of constraints leading to missed deadlines. Data and evaluation biases: experiments with simulated dynamics may not capture unmodeled friction, backlash, or latency in real hardware; limited real-robot experiments risk overfitting hyperparameters (e.g., Savitzky–Golay window) to a specific robot pair. Scalability and compute limits: per-constraint overhead grows with number of link-pairs O(N^2) and may exceed real-time compute budgets for large teams or when using analytic Hessians; decentralized schemes reduce per-robot compute but shrink feasibility regions. Generalization limits: method assumes convex-shape (ellipsoidal) primitives and differentiable scaling functions; nonconvex geometries or contact-rich tasks invalidate safety proofs. Environmental constraints: dynamic external obstacles or unpredictable human motion may require sensor bandwidth and latency beyond tested ranges. Certification limits: formal guarantees require assumptions (accurate state estimates, actuator bounds, solver reliability) which may be violated in practice, limiting provable safety to situations where those assumptions hold.
